A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. All 20 pages of v1.pdf and 24 pages of v2.pdf, including Appendices A–F, support comparison through readable text, equations, tables and figures.

before.justification: v1 reports original MAX-M and Smallest Parent experiments, classification results in Tables 1–3, and CAROT sensitivity experiments in Figure 3.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds SUM-M and HWF-M results in Tables 3–5 and marginal-estimation diagnostics in Figures 3 and 7.

M1.justification: The label-ratio solver, LP pseudo-labeling procedure and CAROT algorithm retain their objectives, constraints and updates. Changing the Section 4.2 heading from integer linear programming to linear programming does not change the procedure: both versions already allow soft labels and an optional integer formulation.

E1.justification: Appendix F adds SUM-M, using sum supervision for MNIST digits, and HWF-M, using expression-value supervision for handwritten digits and operators. HWF also introduces dependent digit/operator positions. These substantially broaden task and input coverage beyond the retained MAX-M and Smallest Parent experiments.

E2.justification: The corresponding MAX-M and Smallest Parent comparisons retain SL, RECORDS and LA. The added scenarios reuse existing comparison methods; RECORDS was not removed from an existing experiment. HWF's LP(GOLD) condition supplies oracle ratios to the existing LP procedure rather than introducing a new competing algorithm.

E3.justification: New SUM experiments use M=5,6,7, imbalance ratios 50/70 and 2,000 training samples. HWF adds 250/1,000-sample settings, a 70%/30% image split and gold-ratio controls. Tables 4–5 report M=3,5,7, conflicting with the prose's M=5,6,7. These are added protocols; the original benchmark settings are retained.

E4.justification: Figures 3 and 7 newly examine Algorithm 1's estimated marginals against gold ratios across transitions and imbalance levels. Appendix F adds demanding small-sample and high-imbalance tests, including oracle-versus-empirical ratio controls for HWF. The original 500-ratio CAROT sensitivity analysis is retained as Figure 4.

E5.justification: Appendix B.3 first discloses ten optimization runs per plotted risk point, rejection of invalid solutions and median aggregation. New Tables 3–5 specify six runs, while the original experiments retain three-run mean-and-standard-deviation reporting. This does not establish increased repetitions of the original experiments.

E6.justification: The original Tables 1–2 and full MAX-M table retain identical results. Substantial new results include SUM-6 at imbalance ratio 50: SL 67.60 versus LP(ALG1) 80.10 in Table 3. Table 5 reports HWF-7 at ratio 15 with 1,000 samples: SL 48.23 versus LP(GOLD) 55.73. These are added evaluations, not improvements over v1 under retained settings.

T1.justification: The risk-bound propositions, consistency proof, non-injectivity counterexample and LP derivation remain unchanged. Section 5 adds a computational-complexity argument contrasting polynomial top-k SL, purportedly NP-hard LP and #P-complete exact SL. No new proof supports this argument, and its LP claim does not distinguish the continuous formulation from the optional integer variant.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain class-specific risk bounds exposing the effect of the transition function, consistent marginal estimation, and training- and testing-time mitigation. The abstract's added 'up to 14%' statement already appeared in v1's introduction. The additional experiments support retained contributions.

C2.justification: v2 expands discussion of training overhead, scalability, class-dependent errors and possible applicability under weak correlations. Appendix F discusses estimation failures and why HWF requires gold ratios. However, its explanation of SUM-7 failure at imbalance ratio 70 cites Figure 7, which displays only ratios 5, 15 and 50.

D1.justification: Appendix B.3 adds the COBYLA solver and risk-plot construction procedure. Appendix F supplies data-generation instructions, matching training/testing class distributions, HWF splitting and classifier information, and SOLAR code-reuse information. Existing hardware, principal libraries and original model descriptions remain unchanged; these disclosures do not establish retuning of retained experiments.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds an explicit distinction from Tang et al.'s similarly named bag-classification setting. Appendix E adds a comparison with multi-instance learning, while other additions cover neurosymbolic applications, noisy-label learning and newer reasoning-shortcut research. The established positioning against long-tail learning and earlier MI-PLL theory remains.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are revised, and the introduction's explanation of supervision strength is moved and expanded in Appendix B.2. v2 adds an appendix roadmap and subheadings, standardizes LP/SOLAR terminology and expands the conclusion. The main section sequence and most methodological and proof text are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a wider page format and enlarges retained tables and plots. It adds three experimental tables and marginal-estimation displays in Figures 3 and 7. Figure 5 enlarges the existing Figure 2; v1's Figures 3–4 become Figures 4 and 6, and its full MAX-M Table 3 becomes Table 6.

improvement.justification: Direct marginal-estimation diagnostics, broader SUM/HWF testing and the procedural disclosures in Appendices B.3/F improve empirical support and transparency. The gain is tempered by HWF's reliance on gold ratios, inconsistencies between its prose and tables, the missing ratio-70 panel cited in the failure analysis, and the ambiguous LP complexity claim. The core algorithms, proofs and original results remain stable.
